questions.title: Threats and measures
questions.text: Match each threat to the measure that best protects against it.

left.text: A hacker tries to connect to the school server from the Internet
A laptop containing pupils' data is stolen
One hard disk in the server fails
A power cut in the server room

scheme.mark_scheme: L1–Firewall, L2–Encryption, L3–Mirroring, L4–UPS. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: Prevent hacking
questions.text: List **three** security measures to prevent hacking.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Any three (1 each): biometric; access control / access rights; antivirus; firewall; double / two-factor authentication; strong password; intranet; encryption; software updates
[max 3] Accept any correct answer
scheme.model_answer: 1 Firewall. 2 Two-factor authentication. 3 Strong passwords.

questions.title: Physical risks
questions.text: Complete the table with **one** countermeasure for each physical risk to a server room.

prefill: Theft of servers
Fire
Power cut
Overheating

scheme.mark_scheme:
Theft (1): locked room / key cards / biometric entry / CCTV / guards
Fire (1): smoke detectors / gas fire-suppression / fireproof safe for backups / off-site backup
Power cut (1): UPS / back-up generator
Overheating (1): air conditioning / temperature monitoring / ventilation
scheme.model_answer: Theft: key-card lock on the door. Fire: gas fire-suppression system. Power cut: UPS. Overheating: air conditioning.

questions.title: Purpose of a UPS
questions.text: Explain the purpose of an **uninterruptible power supply (UPS)** for a server.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- A battery keeps the server running for a short time when the mains power fails (1)
- so data can be saved / the server shut down safely / generator started, preventing data loss or damage (1)

points.criterion: Battery power during a power cut

scheme.model_answer: Its battery keeps the server running for a few minutes when the power fails, so data can be saved and the server shut down safely without losing data.

questions.title: How a firewall works
questions.text: Describe how a **firewall** protects a network.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): monitors / checks data packets entering and leaving the network; compares them with a set of security rules (IP addresses, ports); blocks unauthorised / suspicious packets / connections; logs attempted attacks; can block certain websites
scheme.model_answer: It checks every data packet going in and out of the network against a set of rules, such as allowed IP addresses and ports, and blocks any packet that breaks the rules.

questions.title: Firewall and viruses
questions.text: A firewall scans the files on a hard disk and removes any viruses it finds.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: Removing viruses from files is the job of anti-virus software; a firewall filters network traffic.

questions.title: Encryption
questions.text: Describe how **encryption** protects data.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Data (plaintext) is scrambled into ciphertext using an algorithm and a key (1)
- so if it is intercepted / stolen it cannot be understood without the key (1)
scheme.model_answer: Encryption scrambles the data into ciphertext using a key, so anyone who intercepts or steals it cannot read it without the correct key.

questions.title: Symmetric or asymmetric
questions.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row.

prefill: The same key is used to encrypt and decrypt
A public key encrypts and a private key decrypts
The key has to be shared secretly with the receiver

scheme.mark_scheme: 1 Symmetric (1); 2 Asymmetric (1); 3 Symmetric (1)

questions.title: What encryption does not do
questions.text: A company encrypts all files on its laptops. Which statement is correct?

options.content: The laptops can no longer be stolen
A thief who steals a laptop cannot read the files without the key
The files can no longer be deleted

scheme.mark_scheme: B
scheme.explanation: Encryption makes stolen data unreadable; it does not prevent theft, deletion or malware.

questions.title: Biometric methods
questions.text: Select **two** biometric authentication methods.

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.

questions.title: Biometrics: advantage and disadvantage
questions.text: State **one** advantage and **one** disadvantage of using fingerprint recognition to log in to a computer.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Advantage (1): unique / hard to copy; cannot be forgotten, lost or shared; fast and convenient
Disadvantage (1): expensive hardware; false rejection (dirty / cut finger) / false acceptance; privacy — data cannot be changed if stolen
scheme.model_answer: Advantage: a fingerprint cannot be forgotten or shared like a password. Disadvantage: it may be rejected if the finger is dirty or cut.

questions.title: Two-factor authentication
questions.text: Explain how **two-factor authentication** makes an online bank account more secure.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- The user must provide two different types of evidence, e.g. a password and a code sent to the phone / a fingerprint (1)
- so a hacker who steals / guesses the password still cannot log in without the second factor (1)

points.criterion: Stolen password alone is not enough

scheme.model_answer: After the password, the bank also asks for a one-time code sent to the customer's phone, so a hacker who has stolen the password still cannot log in without the phone.

questions.title: How anti-virus detects malware
questions.text: Describe **two** methods anti-virus software uses to detect malware.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): signature-based — compares files with a database of known virus signatures; heuristic / behaviour analysis — detects suspicious behaviour of programs; real-time scanning of files as they are opened / downloaded
scheme.model_answer: 1 It compares files with a database of signatures of known viruses. 2 It watches for suspicious behaviour, such as a program changing many system files, to catch new viruses.

questions.title: Virus countermeasures
questions.text: State **two** countermeasures, other than installing anti-virus software, that reduce the risk of a computer virus infection.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): keep OS / software updated; do not open unknown attachments / links; scan / disable autorun for USB drives; download only from trusted sources; firewall; limited user accounts; user training; regular backups
scheme.model_answer: 1 Keep the operating system updated. 2 Do not open e-mail attachments from unknown senders.

questions.title: Data backup
questions.text: Describe what is meant by a **data backup**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- A copy of the data made on a separate medium / location (1)
- so it can be restored if the original is lost / damaged / deleted (1)
scheme.model_answer: A copy of data stored on a separate medium, ideally in another place, so it can be restored if the original data is lost or damaged.

questions.title: Types of backup
questions.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show the type of backup described.

prefill: Copies all the data every time
Copies only data changed since the last backup of any type
Copies all data changed since the last full backup

scheme.mark_scheme: 1 Full (1); 2 Incremental (1); 3 Differential (1)

questions.title: Off-site backups
questions.text: Explain why backups should be kept **off-site** (in a different building or in the cloud).

scheme.mark_scheme:
- A fire / flood / theft at the main site would destroy both the original and a backup kept in the same place (1)
- an off-site copy survives, so the data can still be restored (1)

points.criterion: Disaster at one site destroys both

scheme.model_answer: If the building burns down or is flooded, a backup kept in the same room would be destroyed with the original; an off-site copy survives and the data can be restored.

questions.title: Disk mirroring
questions.text: Describe how **disk mirroring** protects data.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Data is written to two (or more) disks at the same time, so they hold identical copies (RAID 1) (1)
- if one disk fails, the system continues from the other disk without data loss / downtime (1)
scheme.model_answer: Every piece of data is written to two disks at the same time, so if one disk fails, the computer keeps working from the identical copy on the other disk.

questions.title: Mirroring vs backup
questions.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show whether the statement describes **backup** or **disk mirroring**.

prefill: Copies data continuously, in real time
Can be used to restore a file deleted by mistake last week
The system keeps working with no downtime when a disk fails
A copy can be stored in another city

scheme.mark_scheme: 1 Mirroring (1); 2 Backup (1); 3 Mirroring (1); 4 Backup (1)

questions.title: Ransomware attack
questions.text:
A small accounting firm stores clients' data on one server with disk mirroring. Last month ransomware encrypted all its files.

Discuss why disk mirroring did not protect the data, and recommend measures the firm should take.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Up to 4 marks:
- Mirroring copies every change immediately, so the encrypted files were written to both disks (1)
- mirroring only protects against disk failure, not malware / deletion (1)
- Regular backups, at least one offline / off-site, to restore unencrypted files (1)
- Anti-virus updated / firewall / OS updates (1)
- Staff training on phishing / not opening attachments; limited user rights (1)
[Max 4]
scheme.model_answer: Disk mirroring writes every change to both disks at once, so when the ransomware encrypted the files, both copies were encrypted; mirroring only protects against a disk failing. The firm should make regular backups and keep one copy offline or off-site so it can restore the original files, install and update anti-virus software and a firewall, keep the system updated, and train staff not to open suspicious attachments.

questions.title: A protection plan for a school
questions.text:
A school stores pupils' personal data and marks on a server connected to the Internet. Teachers take laptops home.

Evaluate the measures the school should use to protect this data. Refer to physical security, firewalls, encryption, biometrics or passwords, anti-virus software, backup and disk mirroring.

scheme.mark_scheme:
One mark per well-explained measure linked to the scenario (max 5), e.g.
- locked server room / UPS / fire protection (physical)
- firewall to block Internet attacks on the server
- encryption of laptops so stolen laptops do not expose data
- strong passwords + 2FA / biometrics for staff log-in, access rights so pupils cannot see marks
- anti-virus with updates against malware
- regular off-site / cloud backups to restore after loss or ransomware
- disk mirroring so the server keeps running if a disk fails
Evaluation / conclusion (1): e.g. no single measure is enough; mirroring is not a backup; cost vs risk
scheme.model_answer: The server should be in a locked room with a UPS, so it cannot be stolen or damaged by a power cut. A firewall should block unauthorised connections from the Internet. Teachers' laptops should be encrypted, so if one is stolen the pupils' data cannot be read. Staff should log in with strong passwords and two-factor authentication, and access rights should stop pupils from seeing marks. Anti-virus software must be kept updated. The server should use disk mirroring so it keeps running if a disk fails, but because mirroring copies deletions and ransomware too, the school also needs regular backups stored off-site. No single measure is enough, so the school should combine them.

questions.title: Protecting a school network
questions.text: A school's server stores pupils' personal data and is connected to the Internet. Teachers also keep pupils' marks on their laptops.

parts.title: Three measures
parts.text: List **three** security measures to prevent hacking.

scheme.mark_scheme: Biometric (1) Access control (1) Antivirus (1) Firewall (1) Use double authentication (1) Use strong password (1) Intranet (1) Encryption (1) [max 3] Accept any correct answer
scheme.model_answer: 1 Firewall. 2 Strong passwords. 3 Two-factor authentication.

parts.title: Firewall
parts.text: Describe how a firewall protects the school server.

scheme.mark_scheme: Checks / monitors packets entering and leaving the network (1); against security rules — IP addresses / ports (1); blocks unauthorised traffic (1) [Max 2]
scheme.model_answer: It checks each packet coming from the Internet against security rules and blocks any connection that is not allowed.

parts.title: Firewall limitation
parts.text: State **one** threat that a firewall cannot protect against.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any one (1): virus on a USB stick / in an allowed e-mail attachment; insider / authorised user misusing data; phishing; physical theft; disk failure
scheme.model_answer: A virus brought in on a USB stick.

parts.title: Encryption
parts.text: Explain how encryption protects the pupils' marks if a teacher's laptop is stolen.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- The data is scrambled with a key / stored as ciphertext (1)
- the thief cannot read / understand the marks without the key (1)
scheme.model_answer: The marks are stored as ciphertext, so the thief cannot read them without the decryption key.

questions.title: Authentication and malware
questions.text: A bank wants to make its staff log-in and computers more secure.

parts.title: Biometric methods
parts.text: State **two** biometric methods the bank could use.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): fingerprint; face recognition; iris / retina scan; voice recognition; hand geometry; signature dynamics
scheme.model_answer: 1 Fingerprint recognition. 2 Iris scan.

parts.title: Biometrics evaluated
parts.text: State **one** advantage and **one** disadvantage of biometrics compared with passwords.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Advantage (1): unique / hard to copy; cannot be forgotten or shared; faster
Disadvantage (1): expensive; false rejections / acceptances; cannot be changed if stolen / privacy
scheme.model_answer: Advantage: it cannot be forgotten or given to another person. Disadvantage: if the biometric data is stolen it cannot be changed like a password.

parts.title: Two-factor authentication
parts.text: Explain how two-factor authentication improves security.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Two different types of evidence are needed (something you know / have / are) (1)
- a stolen password alone is not enough to log in (1)
scheme.model_answer: Staff need a password and also a fingerprint or a code on their phone, so someone who has stolen a password still cannot log in.

parts.title: New viruses
parts.text: Explain how anti-virus software can detect a **new** virus that is not yet in its signature database.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Heuristic / behaviour-based detection (1)
- watches for suspicious actions, e.g. changing system files / copying itself / encrypting many files, and quarantines the program (1)
scheme.model_answer: It uses heuristic analysis: it watches what programs do and blocks one that behaves suspiciously, such as trying to change many system files.

questions.title: The server room
questions.text: A hospital's server room holds the servers with patients' records.

parts.title: Physical risks
parts.text: Draw a line to link each physical risk to the most suitable countermeasure.

right.text: Door opened only by key card and CCTV

scheme.mark_scheme: Theft–R1, Fire–R2, Overheating–R3. One mark per correct line.

parts.title: UPS
parts.text: Explain why the hospital's servers are connected to a UPS.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Battery power keeps the servers running when the mains power fails (1)
- so records are not lost / servers shut down safely / generator can start; patient records remain available (1)
scheme.model_answer: If the power fails, the UPS battery keeps the servers running until the generator starts, so patient records are not lost or damaged.

parts.title: Off-site backup
parts.text: Explain why the hospital keeps a copy of its backups in another building.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- A fire / flood / theft could destroy the servers and any backups in the same room (1)
- the copy in another building survives, so records can be restored (1)
scheme.model_answer: A fire in the server room would destroy both the servers and any backups stored there; a copy in another building can still be used to restore the records.

questions.title: Backup and disk mirroring
questions.text: An online shop uses disk mirroring on its web server and also makes backups.

parts.title: Mirroring
parts.text: Describe disk mirroring.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Data is written to two disks simultaneously / identical copies (1)
- if one disk fails the other is used and the system keeps running (1)
scheme.model_answer: All data is written to two disks at the same time, so if one fails the server keeps running from the other one.

parts.title: Why also backup
parts.text: Explain why the shop also needs backups, even though it uses disk mirroring.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Deletions / corruption / ransomware are copied to both disks immediately (1)
- backups keep earlier copies that can be restored / can be off-site in case of fire or theft (1)
scheme.model_answer: If a file is deleted or encrypted by ransomware, the change is mirrored to both disks at once, so only a backup lets the shop restore an earlier, undamaged copy.

parts.title: Full vs incremental
parts.text: Compare a **full** backup with an **incremental** backup.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each), both sides: full copies all data vs incremental only changes since the last backup; full slower / more space vs incremental faster / less space; full easier / faster to restore vs incremental needs full + every incremental
scheme.model_answer: A full backup copies all the data each time, while an incremental backup copies only what has changed since the last backup, so it is faster and uses less space; however, restoring needs the full backup plus every incremental one.

parts.title: Off-site medium
parts.text: State **one** suitable medium or service for keeping an off-site backup.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any one (1): cloud storage; magnetic tape stored elsewhere; external hard disk kept in another building; remote server / data centre
scheme.model_answer: Cloud storage.

questions.title: Confidentiality, integrity, availability
questions.text: Match each security goal to its meaning.

right.text: The data and system can be used when they are needed
Only authorised people can read the data
The data is correct and changed only by authorised people

scheme.mark_scheme: Confidentiality – Only authorised people can read the data; Integrity – The data is correct and changed only by authorised people; Availability – The data and system can be used when they are needed. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: Power cut
questions.text: Which device keeps a server running for a few minutes when the mains power fails?

scheme.mark_scheme: B

questions.title: UPS or surge protector
questions.text: Explain the difference between a **UPS** and a **surge protector**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- A UPS has a battery that keeps the computer running when the power fails (1)
- a surge protector only stops voltage spikes damaging the computer; it does not keep it running (1)

points.criterion: A UPS has a battery that keeps the computer running when the power fails
a surge protector only stops voltage spikes damaging the computer; it does not keep it running

scheme.model_answer: A UPS uses a battery to keep the computer running in a power cut; a surge protector only blocks sudden voltage spikes and gives no power when the mains fails.

questions.title: Apply the firewall rules
questions.text:
A school firewall has these rules: **1** allow port 443 (HTTPS) from anywhere; **2** allow port 22 (SSH) only from the IT office; **3** block port 3306 (MySQL) from outside the school; **4** block everything else.

Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show what happens to each connection.

prefill: A parent opens the school website (port 443)
A computer outside the school connects to port 3306
The IT office connects to port 22
A home computer connects to port 22

scheme.mark_scheme: A parent opens the school website (port 443) – Allowed (1); A computer outside the school connects to port 3306 – Blocked (1); The IT office connects to port 22 – Allowed (1); A home computer connects to port 22 – Blocked (1)

questions.title: What a firewall cannot do
questions.text: State **two** threats that a firewall **cannot** protect a school network against.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Any one of: malware in an e-mail attachment / allowed traffic; virus on a USB stick; an insider already in the network; stolen / weak passwords; physical theft or fire (1)
A second, different threat (1)

points.criterion: Any one of: malware in an e-mail attachment / allowed traffic; virus on a USB stick; an insider already in the network; stolen / weak passwords; physical theft or fire

scheme.model_answer: A virus brought in on a USB stick, and a member of staff inside the network misusing their access.

questions.title: Hardware or software firewall
questions.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row.

prefill: Protects the whole school network at the connection to the Internet
Is a program installed on one laptop
Can decide which programs on a computer may use the network

scheme.mark_scheme: Protects the whole school network at the connection to the Internet – Hardware firewall (1); Is a program installed on one laptop – Software firewall (1); Can decide which programs on a computer may use the network – Software firewall (1)

questions.title: Caesar cipher
questions.text:
A Caesar cipher shifts every letter **3** places forward in the alphabet (A → D, B → E, … X → A, Y → B, Z → C).

Encrypt the word `DOG`: [[1]]

Decrypt the ciphertext `FRGH`: [[2]]

scheme.mark_scheme: (1) GRJ (2) CODE

questions.title: HTTPS
questions.text: HTTPS uses asymmetric encryption to send a symmetric session key safely, then encrypts the rest of the data with the symmetric key.

scheme.mark_scheme: True.
scheme.explanation: Asymmetric encryption solves the problem of sharing the key; symmetric encryption is then used because it is faster.

questions.title: Losing the key
questions.text: A company encrypts all its laptops. Explain the problem if an employee forgets the encryption password, and **one** way the company can prepare for this.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- The data cannot be decrypted / is lost — it cannot be read without the key (1)
- Keep a recovery key / key backup stored securely by the IT department (1)

points.criterion: The data cannot be decrypted / is lost — it cannot be read without the key
Keep a recovery key / key backup stored securely by the IT department

scheme.model_answer: Without the key the encrypted data cannot be read, so it is effectively lost; the IT department should keep a recovery key in a secure place.

questions.title: How biometrics works
questions.text:
Complete the sentences.

When a user registers, their fingerprint is scanned during [[1]] and its features are stored as a [[2]]. When the user logs in, the new scan is [[3]] with the stored features.

scheme.mark_scheme: (1) enrolment (2) template (3) compared

questions.title: False rejection and false acceptance
questions.text: Explain the difference between a **false rejection** and a **false acceptance** in a biometric system, and state which is more dangerous.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- False rejection: an authorised user is refused (1)
- False acceptance: an unauthorised person is let in (1)
- False acceptance is more dangerous (security breach) (1)

points.criterion: False rejection: an authorised user is refused
False acceptance: an unauthorised person is let in
False acceptance is more dangerous (security breach)

scheme.model_answer: A false rejection refuses the real user; a false acceptance lets someone else in. A false acceptance is more dangerous because it is a security breach.

questions.title: Authentication factors
questions.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show the type of authentication factor.

prefill: PIN code
Fingerprint
Bank card
Code from an app on your phone

scheme.mark_scheme: PIN code – Something you know (1); Fingerprint – Something you are (1); Bank card – Something you have (1); Code from an app on your phone – Something you have (1)

questions.title: Password and PIN
questions.text: Asking a user for a password and then a PIN is an example of two-factor authentication.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: Both are 'something you know'. Two-factor authentication needs two different types of factor.

questions.title: Signature and heuristic detection
questions.text: Compare **signature-based** and **heuristic** detection of malware.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Signature-based compares files with a database of known malware, so it cannot detect new malware (1)
- Heuristic looks for suspicious behaviour / code, so it can detect new malware but gives more false alarms (1)

points.criterion: Signature-based compares files with a database of known malware, so it cannot detect new malware
Heuristic looks for suspicious behaviour / code, so it can detect new malware but gives more false alarms

scheme.model_answer: Signature-based detection matches files against known malware signatures and misses new malware; heuristic detection watches for suspicious behaviour, so it can find new malware but may raise false alarms.

questions.title: Quarantine
questions.text: What does anti-virus software do when it **quarantines** a file?

options.content: Deletes every file in the same folder
Moves the file to a safe area where it cannot run
Sends the file to the user's e-mail

scheme.mark_scheme: B

questions.title: Out-of-date anti-virus
questions.text: Anti-virus software whose signature database has not been updated for a year can still detect every virus released this month.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: Signature-based detection only knows malware that is in its database, so new viruses are missed until the database is updated.

questions.title: Worm and Trojan
questions.text: Describe how a **worm** and a **Trojan** get onto a computer.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Worm: copies itself across the network through security holes, without the user doing anything (1)
Trojan: the user installs it, believing it is useful software (1)

points.criterion: Worm: copies itself across the network through security holes, without the user doing anything
Trojan: the user installs it, believing it is useful software

scheme.model_answer: A worm spreads by itself across the network through security holes; a Trojan is installed by the user, who thinks it is a useful program.

questions.title: An infected computer
questions.text: A teacher's computer is infected with malware. Describe **three** steps the IT technician should take.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Disconnect the computer from the network (1)
- Run a full scan with updated anti-virus / quarantine or delete infected files (1)
- Change passwords / restore files from a clean backup / find and fix how it got in (1)

points.criterion: Disconnect the computer from the network
Run a full scan with updated anti-virus / quarantine or delete infected files
Change passwords / restore files from a clean backup / find and fix how it got in

scheme.model_answer: Disconnect it from the network, run a full scan with updated anti-virus software and remove the malware, then restore damaged files from a backup and change the passwords.

questions.title: Restoring incremental backups
questions.text: A full backup is made on Sunday night and **incremental** backups on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday nights. The disk fails on Thursday morning. Which backups are needed to restore the data?

scheme.mark_scheme: C

questions.title: Restoring differential backups
questions.text: A full backup is made on Sunday night and **differential** backups on Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday nights. The disk fails on Thursday morning. Which backups are needed to restore the data?

scheme.mark_scheme: D

questions.title: The 3-2-1 rule
questions.text:
Complete the 3-2-1 backup rule.

Keep [[1]] copies of the data, on [[2]] different types of media, with [[3]] copy stored off-site.

questions.title: Cloud backup
questions.text: State **one** advantage and **one** disadvantage of backing up a school's data to cloud storage.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Advantage, e.g. automatically off-site / safe from fire or theft / no hardware to manage / restore from anywhere (1)
Disadvantage, e.g. needs a reliable Internet connection / ongoing cost / data held by another company (privacy) / slow to restore (1)

points.criterion: Advantage, e.g. automatically off-site / safe from fire or theft / no hardware to manage / restore from anywhere
Disadvantage, e.g. needs a reliable Internet connection / ongoing cost / data held by another company (privacy) / slow to restore

scheme.model_answer: The backup is automatically off-site, but it needs a fast Internet connection to back up and restore.

questions.title: Mirroring and ransomware
questions.text: Disk mirroring protects a company's files if ransomware encrypts them.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: The encrypted files are written to both mirrored disks at once; only a backup made before the attack can restore them.

questions.title: RAID 0
questions.text: A server uses **RAID 0** (striping) on two disks, and one disk fails. What happens?

options.content: The server keeps working from the other disk
The data is rebuilt from parity information
The data on the array is lost
Nothing — RAID 0 makes a backup every night

scheme.mark_scheme: C

questions.title: Plan backups for a shop
questions.text: A small shop records all its sales in a database on one computer. Suggest a backup plan for the shop. Your answer should state **how often** to back up, the **type** of backup and **where** the copies are kept.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- How often, e.g. automatically every night / every day after closing (1)
- Type, e.g. weekly full plus nightly incremental or differential (1)
- Where, e.g. one copy off-site or in the cloud, kept offline / away from the shop computer (1)

points.criterion: How often, e.g. automatically every night / every day after closing
Type, e.g. weekly full plus nightly incremental or differential
Where, e.g. one copy off-site or in the cloud, kept offline / away from the shop computer

scheme.model_answer: Back up automatically every night after closing: a full backup each Sunday and incremental backups on the other nights, kept on an external disk and also in cloud storage, so one copy is off-site.

questions.title: Which rule decides?
questions.text:
A school firewall has these rules, checked from the top: **1** allow port 443 from anywhere; **2** allow port 22 only from the IT office; **3** block port 3306 from the Internet; **4** block everything else.

A computer on the Internet tries to connect to port **22**. Which rule decides what happens?

scheme.mark_scheme: D

questions.title: Why the Caesar cipher is weak
questions.text: Explain why a message encrypted with a Caesar cipher can be broken quickly, even without the key.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- There are only 25 possible keys / shifts (1)
- an attacker can try them all (brute force) and pick the message that makes sense (1)

points.criterion: There are only 25 possible keys / shifts
an attacker can try them all (brute force) and pick the message that makes sense

scheme.model_answer: There are only 25 possible shifts, so an attacker tries all of them and reads the one that makes sense.

questions.title: Strongest password
questions.text: Which password is the most difficult to crack?

scheme.mark_scheme: D

questions.title: Account lockout
questions.text: Explain how **locking an account after five wrong passwords** protects it against a brute-force attack.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- A brute-force attack tries very many passwords one after another (1)

summary: Measures that protect data and computer systems — protection against physical risks, firewalls (inter-network screens), encryption, biometrics and anti-virus countermeasures — and using data backup and disk mirroring (RAID 1) to keep data safe.

blocks.content: Data and computer systems are at risk from **people** (hackers, thieves, careless users), **malicious software** and **physical events** (fire, flood, power cuts, hardware failure). No single measure protects against everything, so organisations use **several layers of protection** ("defence in depth").

blocks.title: Threats and the measures that protect against them
rows: Fire, flood, power cut, theft of hardware
**Physical security**, UPS, fire-suppression systems, **backup** stored off-site
Interception of data in transit, stolen laptops

blocks.text: What we are protecting: confidentiality, integrity, availability

items.title: Confidentiality
items.content: Only **authorised** people can **read** the data. Broken when a hacker reads pupils' marks or a laptop with customers' data is stolen. Protected by **access rights, passwords, encryption**.

items.title: Integrity
items.content: The data is **correct and complete** and is changed only by authorised people. Broken when a virus corrupts files or a pupil changes marks. Protected by **access rights, validation, anti-virus, backups**.

items.title: Availability
items.content: The data and the system can be **used when they are needed**. Broken by a power cut, a failed disk or ransomware. Protected by **UPS, disk mirroring, backups**.

blocks.title: Layers of protection for a school server
blocks.content:
1. **Physical:** the server is in a locked, air-conditioned room with a UPS.
2. **Network:** a firewall between the school network and the Internet.
3. **Access:** every user has their own account, a strong password and only the rights they need.
4. **Data:** sensitive data is encrypted; anti-virus scans every file.
5. **Recovery:** disks are mirrored and a backup is made every night and kept off-site.

If one layer fails — for example a teacher's password is stolen — the other layers still protect the data.

blocks.title: Physical risks and countermeasures
rows: Locked server rooms, security guards, CCTV, cable locks, entry by key card or biometrics, visitor logs
Smoke detectors, gas-based fire-suppression systems (no water near computers), fireproof safes for backups
Servers not in basements, raised floors, water sensors
**Uninterruptible power supply (UPS)**, surge protectors, back-up generators
Air conditioning, temperature monitoring in server rooms
Disk mirroring (RAID), spare parts, regular maintenance
No food or drink near computers, protective cases, user training

blocks.content: A device with a **battery** that keeps computers running for a short time when the mains power fails, so that work can be **saved** and the system **shut down safely** (or a generator started).

blocks.title: What happens in a power cut
items: The mains power fails — the **UPS battery** takes over at once, so the server does not switch off.
The UPS tells the server that it is running on battery.
Users have a few minutes to **save** their work; the server **shuts down safely** if the power does not return (or a **generator** starts).
Without a UPS, files being written could be **corrupted** and unsaved work **lost**.

blocks.content: A device that stops a sudden **spike in voltage** (for example from lightning) from reaching and damaging the computer. Unlike a UPS, it does **not** keep the computer running when the power fails.

Hardware or software that **monitors all data packets passing between a private network (or computer) and the outside network (Internet)** and **allows or blocks** them according to a set of **security rules**. It is the "screen" between two networks.

flowchart TB
  I[Internet] <--> F{Firewall: check each packet against the rules}
  F <--> N[School network: servers and PCs]
  F -. blocked .-> X[Unauthorised connection]
blocks.caption: A firewall sits between the internal network and the Internet

items.title: What a firewall does
items.content:
- Checks the **source and destination IP address**, **port number** and protocol of every packet.
- **Blocks** packets that do not match the rules (e.g. connections to unused ports, known bad addresses).
- Can **block access** to certain websites or applications.
- **Logs** attempts to connect, so attacks can be investigated.
- Can hide the internal addresses of the network from outsiders.

items.title: Limitations
items.content:
- Cannot stop malware that arrives through **allowed** channels (e-mail attachments, USB sticks).
- Does not protect against **insiders** already inside the network.
- Must be **configured correctly** — bad rules either block useful traffic or let attacks through.

blocks.title: Hardware and software firewalls
rows: A separate device (often in the router) between the network and the Internet
A program on each computer, e.g. Windows Defender Firewall
Traffic in and out of the network
Which **programs** on that computer may use the network
Home users, laptops used on public Wi-Fi

blocks.title: Firewall rules for a school web server
blocks.content:
| Rule | Port / service | Source | Action |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 443 (HTTPS — the school website) | Any | **Allow** |
| 2 | 22 (SSH — remote administration) | Only the IT office's IP address | **Allow** |
| 3 | 3306 (MySQL database) | Any address outside the school | **Block** |
| 4 | Everything else | Any | **Block** |

A visitor opening the website is allowed (rule 1). A hacker trying to log in to the database from outside is blocked (rule 3). The last rule blocks everything that is not allowed — "deny by default".

Converting data (**plaintext**) into an unreadable form (**ciphertext**) using an **algorithm** and a **key**, so that only someone with the correct key can **decrypt** it and read it. Encryption does **not** stop data being stolen, but makes stolen data **useless** to the thief.

flowchart TB
  P[Plaintext: Exam on Monday] -->|encrypt with key| C[Ciphertext: Q8#k2!zP...]
  C -->|send over the Internet| C2[Ciphertext received]
  C2 -->|decrypt with key| P2[Plaintext: Exam on Monday]
blocks.caption: Encrypting and decrypting a message

blocks.title: Symmetric and asymmetric encryption
rows: A **public key** encrypts, a **private key** decrypts
Solves key sharing — the public key can be given to anyone

items.title: Where encryption is used
items.content:
- **HTTPS / SSL / TLS** — web pages, online banking, payments.
- **Full-disk encryption** on laptops and phones, encrypted USB drives.
- **Wi-Fi** (WPA2 / WPA3).
- Messaging apps with end-to-end encryption.
- Storing **passwords** as hashes (one-way) rather than plain text.

items.title: Advantages and disadvantages
items.content:
- ✔ Stolen or intercepted data cannot be read.
- ✔ Protects data on lost devices.
- ✘ If the **key is lost**, the data is lost too.
- ✘ Takes processing time; does not stop deletion or ransomware.

blocks.text: A simple cipher: the Caesar cipher

blocks.title: Shift each letter 3 places forward
blocks.content:
| Plain | A | B | C | … | X | Y | Z |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Cipher | D | E | F | … | A | B | C |

`CAT` → `FDW`; `HELLO` → `KHOOR`. The **algorithm** is "shift the letters"; the **key** is **3**. To decrypt, shift back by 3. With only 25 possible keys it is broken in seconds by trying all of them (**brute force**) — real encryption uses keys with billions of billions of possibilities.

blocks.title: Encrypt, decrypt and break a Caesar cipher
How HTTPS uses both kinds of encryption
items: The browser connects to `https://` and receives the website's **public key** (in its digital certificate).
The browser creates a **session key** and sends it **encrypted with the public key** — only the website's **private key** can decrypt it (**asymmetric**).
From then on, all data is encrypted with the fast **symmetric** session key.
Result: the key is shared safely **and** the data travels quickly.

theory.title: Exam practice: threats, firewalls and encryption

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: State one threat that a firewall cannot protect against. [1]**
Malware in an e-mail attachment or on a USB stick / an insider already in the network / weak passwords.

**Q: Explain how encryption protects pupils' marks if a teacher's laptop is stolen. [2]**
The data is stored as **ciphertext** (1); the thief cannot read it without the **key / password** (1).

**Q: Explain why a server is connected to a UPS. [2]**
If the power fails, the UPS **battery keeps the server running** (1) so data can be saved and the server **shut down safely** — no corruption or data loss (1).

Authentication using **unique physical or behavioural characteristics** of a person, which are compared with a stored **template**. Examples: **fingerprint**, **face recognition**, **iris / retina scan**, **voice recognition**, **hand geometry**, **signature dynamics**.

blocks.title: How biometric authentication works
items: **Enrolment:** the user's fingerprint (face, iris…) is scanned several times; the important features are turned into a **template** and stored — the image itself is usually not kept.
**Log-in:** a new scan is made and turned into features in the same way.
**Matching:** the new features are **compared** with the template and a **similarity score** is calculated.
**Decision:** if the score is above a **threshold**, access is allowed; otherwise it is refused.

blocks.title: False rejection and false acceptance
rows: Your phone does not recognise your wet finger
Someone else's face unlocks your phone

blocks.title: Biometric methods
rows: Sensor reads the ridges of a finger
Cheap, fast; dirty or cut fingers can fail
Contactless; lighting, glasses or masks can affect it
Camera scans the pattern of the eye
Very accurate; expensive; some users dislike it
A cold or background noise can cause rejection

items.title: Advantages
items.content:
- Characteristics are **unique** and hard to **copy or guess**.
- **Cannot be forgotten, lost or shared** like a password or card.
- Fast and convenient to use.
- Gives an **audit trail** of exactly who entered.

items.title: Disadvantages
items.content:
- **Expensive** hardware.
- **False rejections** (an authorised user is refused) and **false acceptances**.
- **Privacy** concerns — biometric data is personal; if stolen it **cannot be changed** like a password.
- Some characteristics change (injury, age).

blocks.title: Two-factor authentication (2FA)
blocks.content: Combining **two different types** of evidence — something you **know** (password), something you **have** (phone, card) and something you **are** (biometric) — makes unauthorised access much harder. Example: a password plus a code sent to your phone.

blocks.title: The three authentication factors
rows: Password, PIN, answer to a security question
Can be guessed, stolen by phishing, forgotten
Phone (SMS code, app), bank card, key card, USB token
False acceptance / rejection; cannot be changed if leaked

blocks.content: A password **and** a PIN are both "something you know" — this is **not** two-factor authentication. 2FA needs factors of **different types**.
Biometrics prove **who** a user is, but most systems still rely on **passwords** — and on giving each user only the access they need.

items.title: A strong password
items.content:
- **Long** — at least 12 characters; length matters most.
- Mixes **upper and lower case, digits and symbols**.
- **Not** a dictionary word, name, date of birth or keyboard pattern (`qwerty`, `123456`).
- **Different** for every account, so one leak does not open the others.
- Kept in a **password manager**, not on a sticky note.

items.title: A password policy (set by the organisation)
items.content:
- Minimum length and required character types.
- **Account lockout** after a few wrong attempts (e.g. 5), which stops brute-force attacks.
- Passwords are stored as **hashes**, never as plain text.
- Passwords are changed **at once** if they may have leaked.
- **Two-factor authentication** for important accounts (e-mail, banking, administrators).

blocks.title: How long would a brute-force attack take?

blocks.content: Rules set by the administrator that decide **what each user may do** with each file, folder or table: **no access**, **read only**, **read and write (change)**, or **full control** (also delete and change permissions).

blocks.title: Access rights in a school information system
blocks.content:
| User | Pupils' marks | Pupils' personal data | Staff salaries |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pupil | Read **own** marks only | Read **own** data only | No access |
| Teacher | Read and write for **their classes** | Read for their classes | No access |
| Accountant | No access | No access | Read and write |
| Administrator | Full control | Full control | Full control |

items.title: Principle of least privilege
items.content: Every user gets **only the access needed for their job** — no more. If an account is stolen or a user makes a mistake, the damage is limited to that small area.

items.title: Audit trail (log)
items.content: The system **records who did what and when** (logged in, opened, changed, deleted). Logs help to find the cause of a problem and discourage misuse.

items.title: Smart cards and tokens
items.content: A **smart card** or USB **security key** contains a chip that proves the user has it ("something you have"). A **one-time password (OTP)** from an app or SMS changes every 30–60 seconds, so a stolen code is soon useless.

blocks.content: A utility program that **scans** files, e-mails, downloads and memory to **detect, quarantine and remove malware** (viruses, worms, Trojans, spyware, ransomware).

blocks.title: Malware and how it spreads
rows: Attaches itself to files or programs and damages data
Runs when the infected file is opened; USB drives, e-mail
Copies itself across a network by itself
Network security holes — no user action needed
Pretends to be useful software but harms the computer
The user downloads and installs it

blocks.title: How anti-virus software works
items: **Signature-based detection** — compares files with a database of known malware **signatures**; the database must be **updated** regularly.
**Heuristic / behaviour analysis** — detects **suspicious behaviour** (e.g. a program trying to change many system files), so it can catch new malware.
**Real-time (on-access) scanning** checks files as they are opened or downloaded.
Infected files are **quarantined** (isolated) or **deleted**; the user is warned.

blocks.title: Other virus countermeasures
rows: Fixes security holes that malware uses
Many viruses spread by e-mail and phishing
Scan **USB drives** before use; disable autorun
Malware cannot easily spread or change the system
Files can be restored after ransomware
People recognise phishing and suspicious files

blocks.title: Signature-based vs heuristic detection
rows: Compares files with a database of **known** malware signatures
**No** — only malware already in the database
More — a normal program may look suspicious

blocks.title: What to do if a computer is infected
items: **Disconnect** it from the network so the malware cannot spread.
Run a **full scan** with updated anti-virus software; **quarantine / delete** infected files.
**Change passwords** that may have been stolen (from a clean computer).
**Restore** damaged files from a clean **backup**.
Find out **how** it got in (attachment, USB, missing update) and fix the cause.

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: State two biometric methods. [2]**
Any two: fingerprint, face recognition, iris / retina scan, voice recognition, hand geometry.

**Q: Explain how two-factor authentication improves security. [2]**
The user must give **two different types** of evidence, e.g. a password **and** a code sent to their phone (1); a criminal who steals the password still **cannot log in without the phone** (1).

**Q: Explain how anti-virus software can detect a new virus that is not in its signature database. [2]**
**Heuristic / behaviour analysis** (1): it watches for suspicious actions, such as a program changing many system files, and blocks it (1).

A **copy of data** stored on a **separate medium**, preferably in a **different location**, so that the original can be **restored** if it is lost, damaged, deleted, stolen or encrypted by ransomware.

blocks.title: Types of backup
rows: Only data changed **since the last backup of any type**
Slowest — the full backup **plus every** incremental one
Data changed **since the last full** backup

blocks.title: Restoring after a failure on Thursday morning
blocks.content:
A full backup is made on **Sunday** night; from Monday to Wednesday a backup is made every night. The disk fails on **Thursday** morning.

| Method used Mon–Wed | Backups needed to restore |
|---|---|
| **Incremental** | Sunday full **+ Monday + Tuesday + Wednesday** incrementals (all of them, in order) |
| **Differential** | Sunday full **+ Wednesday** differential only |

Work done on Thursday before the failure is **lost** in both cases — it was never backed up.

blocks.title: Choose the method and the day of the failure

items.title: A good backup strategy
items.content:
- Back up **regularly** and **automatically** (e.g. every night), at a time when the system is not busy.
- **3-2-1 rule:** keep **3** copies of the data, on **2** different types of media, with **1** copy **off-site** (or in the cloud).
- Keep at least one copy **offline**, so ransomware cannot encrypt it.
- **Encrypt** backups and keep them physically secure.
- **Test** restoring from the backup regularly.

items.title: Backup media
items.content:
- External hard disks / SSDs.
- Magnetic **tape** (cheap for very large amounts, used by companies).
- **Cloud storage** — off-site automatically; needs an Internet connection.
- Network-attached storage (NAS).

blocks.title: Cloud backup
rows: **Off-site automatically** — safe from fire or theft at school
No hardware to buy or look after
**Monthly cost** that grows with the amount of data
Data is held by **another company** — privacy and law (where are the servers?)
Restoring a lot of data can be **slow**

blocks.title: A backup plan for a small shop
blocks.content:
- **Every night at 23:00**: incremental backup of the sales database to a NAS in the office.
- **Every Sunday**: full backup to the NAS **and** to cloud storage (the off-site copy).
- **Once a month**: test that a file can really be restored.
- The NAS is not shared with ordinary users, so ransomware on a till computer cannot reach it.

Data is written to **two (or more) disks at the same time**, so that every disk holds an **identical copy**. If one disk **fails**, the system **continues working** from the other disk **without losing data or stopping**.

write "file.docx"
                      |
              +-------+-------+
              |               |
        +-----------+   +-----------+
        |  Disk 1   |   |  Disk 2   |
        | file.docx |   | file.docx |     identical copies
        +-----------+   +-----------+
   Disk 1 fails  ->  the server keeps running from Disk 2
blocks.caption: Disk mirroring: every write goes to both disks

blocks.title: Backup vs disk mirroring
rows: Deletion, corruption, ransomware, fire, theft (if off-site), disk failure
Data is **restored** — some downtime; changes since the last backup are lost
Yes — you can go back to an earlier copy
No — a deletion or virus is **copied to both disks instantly**
Needs at least **double** the disk space

blocks.content: If a file is **deleted**, **corrupted** or **encrypted by ransomware**, the change is mirrored to **both** disks at once. Organisations therefore use **both**: mirroring for **availability** and backups for **recovery**.

blocks.title: RAID levels you may meet
rows: Data is split across disks for **speed**
Every disk holds an identical copy
Work continues from the other disk
Data and **parity** information are spread over 3 or more disks
The lost disk's data is **rebuilt** from the others

blocks.title: Hot-swapping
blocks.content: In servers the failed disk can often be **replaced while the system keeps running** (hot-swap); the RAID controller then copies the data onto the new disk.
A written plan of **how an organisation will restore its systems and data and continue working** after a serious incident — fire, flood, ransomware, a failed server or a long power cut.

items.title: What the plan contains
items.content:
- A list of the **critical systems and data**, in order of importance.
- **Where the backups are** and **how to restore** them, step by step.
- **Who is responsible** for each task, with contact details.
- **How long** each system may be unavailable, and **how much recent data** may be lost (e.g. "at most one day of sales").
- **Alternative arrangements**: spare equipment, a second site, working on paper.
- How and when the plan is **tested**.

items.title: Why it matters
items.content:
- Decisions are made **in advance**, calmly, not during the crisis.
- Systems come back **faster**, so less money and trust are lost.
- Staff know **exactly what to do**.
- A plan that is **never tested** may fail when it is needed.

blocks.title: Backup vs archive
rows: **Restore** data after it is lost or damaged
**Keep old data** that is no longer used every day, for the long term
A **copy** — the original stays in use
The data is **moved** off the working system
Replaced regularly (e.g. kept for a few weeks)
Kept for **years** (e.g. pupils' records after they leave, old accounts by law)
Last night's copy of the school database
Records of pupils who left school five years ago

blocks.title: Ransomware at a college — recovery in practice
blocks.content:
1. Staff see that files will not open and a ransom note appears.
2. The IT team **disconnects** the infected computers and the server from the network.
3. They follow the **disaster recovery plan**: the server is wiped and the system reinstalled.
4. Data is restored from the **offline backup** made the night before; mirroring did not help, because the encrypted files were copied to both disks.
5. Lessons continue the next day; only half a day of work is lost. **No ransom is paid.**

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: List three security measures to prevent hacking. [3]**
Firewall (1); strong passwords / two-factor authentication (1); biometrics / access control / anti-virus / encryption (1).

**Q: Describe how a firewall protects a school network. [2]**
It checks every **data packet** entering and leaving the network against **security rules** (1) and **blocks** packets from unauthorised sources / to unused ports (1).

**Q: Explain why a company should use both disk mirroring and backup. [2]**
Mirroring keeps the system **running without data loss if a disk fails** (1), but a deletion or virus is copied to both disks, so a **backup** is needed to **restore earlier, undamaged copies** (1).

**Q: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of using fingerprints to log in. [2]**
Advantage: fingerprints are **unique** and **cannot be forgotten or shared** (1). Disadvantage: **false rejections** if the finger is dirty or cut / biometric data cannot be changed if stolen (1).

- Saying a firewall **removes viruses** — that is anti-virus software; a firewall **filters network traffic**.
- Saying encryption **stops data being stolen** — it makes stolen data **unreadable**.
- Treating disk mirroring as a backup (see above).
- Keeping the backup **in the same room** as the original — a fire destroys both.
- Giving vague answers such as "use security" — name the **specific** measure and **what it does**.
